concepts.def: The balance between incoming shortwave solar radiation and outgoing longwave radiation; a surplus at low latitudes and deficit at the poles drives circulation.
The Hadley, Ferrel and Polar cells redistribute heat from the equator towards the poles, creating belts of high and low pressure.
A large body of air with broadly uniform temperature and humidity, classified by its source region, such as tropical maritime or polar continental.
A mid-latitude low-pressure system formed where warm and cold air masses meet, bringing fronts, cloud, rainfall and strong winds.
A high-pressure system with descending, diverging air giving settled, dry conditions — hot and sunny in summer, frosty or foggy in winter.
Boundaries between air masses; at a warm front warm air rises gently over cold air, while a cold front undercuts steeply, giving heavier showers.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Physical Geography: Atmosphere — a core area of A-Level Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Physical Geography: Atmosphere brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Physical Geography: Atmosphere.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which circulation cell lies between the equator and roughly 30 degrees latitude?
options: The Hadley cell
The Ferrel cell
The Polar cell
The Walker cell

mcqs.q: A tropical maritime air mass reaching the British Isles is typically:
options: Warm and moist
Cold and dry
Hot and dry
Cold and moist
Warm air rises gradually over colder air, giving layered cloud and steady rain
Cold air rises steeply over warm air
Air descends, giving clear skies
Pressure always rises sharply

mcqs.q: Winter anticyclones over the British Isles often bring:
options: Cold, clear conditions with frost and fog
Prolonged heavy rainfall
Hurricane-force winds
Warm, humid thunderstorms

mcqs.q: Is the equator hotter because it is closer to the Sun?
options: Fronts are barriers built to keep out cold weather.
The equator is hot because of heat escaping from volcanoes.
No — the equator is hotter because the Sun's rays strike more directly, concentrating energy on a smaller area and passing through less atmosphere.
Tropical regions are hot because they are significantly nearer to the Sun.

mcqs.q: Does high pressure mean stormy weather?
options: Fronts are barriers built to keep out cold weather.
No — in anticyclones air descends and warms, suppressing cloud formation, so conditions are usually dry and settled; storms come with low pressure systems.
High pressure presses harder on clouds and squeezes more rain out of them.
High pressure only occurs at night.

mcqs.q: Is a front just a line where rain happens?
options: Fronts are barriers built to keep out cold weather.
Fronts are bands of rain that move around independently of air masses.
High pressure only occurs at night.
A front is a boundary between air masses of different temperature and humidity; rain occurs because the warmer, lighter air is forced to rise and cool along it.
